title: The Aviator
full_review:
If anyone had any doubts about Leonardo DiCaprio's standing as an honest-to-goodness old-fashioned star, director Martin Scorsese's "The Aviator" (Miramax) should dispel them all.

DiCaprio, who's on screen almost every minute of this epic film, is utterly convincing as the legendary billionaire aviator, inventor, Hollywood producer and industrialist Howard Hughes.

A brief childhood prologue shows him being washed in an oddly erotic manner by an overly attentive mother, who hypnotically warns him that he is "not safe." The action then flashes forward to the late 1920s as Hughes, at his most manic, is directing his huge World War I war epic, "Hell's Angels," spending money hand over fist to get every detail right. (John Logan's script concentrates on the most glamorous years of Hughes' life -- the 1920s through the 1940s -- though Hughes, in fact, lived till 1976.)

After nearly three years of production, Hughes must spend even more money converting "Hell's Angels" to a sound film, when "The Jazz Singer" effectively puts an end to the silent film era, but the film ultimately opens in triumph.

Clearly a ladies man, he soon falls under the spell of a fellow maverick, actress Katharine Hepburn (Cate Blanchett), though their relationship is strained when she brings him home to Connecticut to meet the family, a superior bunch who treat him in a condescending manner. Later, she tells him she's met someone else, and leaves him. He becomes infatuated with B actress Faith Domerque (Kelli Garner), followed by Ava Gardner (Kate Beckinsale).

His Hollywood career continues with "Scarface" and the then-notorious "The Outlaw," in which actress Jane Russell's well-publicized decolletage -- showcased in a bra which he specially designed -- brought him into conflict with the Motion Picture Association censors. He wins the battle by proving that the association approved other films with equal cleavage on display.

His great love -- aviation -- drives him to invent various aircraft (the H-1 Racer, the XF-11 spy plane, and the giant seaplane, the Hercules), set speed records, circle the world in four days and take over TWA.

At the same time, he copes with partial deafness, battles psychological demons stemming from his childhood, and develops germ phobias and peculiar proclivities about various foods and milk. His behavior turns more and more strange, and he becomes a hermit, living in reclusive squalor without clothes (a little rear nudity here), collecting his urine in milk bottles. Other unpleasant aspects of Hughes' personality are touched on unflinchingly: his obsessive-compulsive disorders, his bouts of intense paranoia and his underhanded wiretapping of the women in his life.

The production design is splendid, and the aerial sequences are among the most thrilling ever filmed. One of the most exciting sequences involves his plane stalling when testing the XF-11 and having to make a terrifying crash landing, ripping off the roofs of Beverly Hills homes, and leaving him with burns over much of his body.

After learning that Hughes is going to start trans-Atlantic flights, PanAm's president, Juan Trippe (Alec Baldwin), Hughes' chief rival and adversary, contrives through his buddy, Maine Sen. Owen Brewster (Alan Alda in a superb portrayal), to have him brought up in front of Congress in 1947 to testify about wartime contracts and "defrauding the American public."

In reality, Trippe wants to sustain PanAm's monopoly on those flights, the revelation of which allows Hughes to leave the Senate chambers in triumph.

Some of the period details -- re-creations of the Coconut Grove, for instance -- seem more cliched than truly authentic, but this is minor carping for such a visually rich cavalcade.

The film ends rather abruptly on a career highpoint, but with troublesome harbingers of future psychological trouble, and not even a postscript about what happens to Hughes later in life. After nearly three hours, it's remarkable that you can still be left wanting more.

This is one of the most commercial films of Scorsese's career. The film maintains a terrific momentum, and the Scorsese stamp is unmistakable, several of the scenes leaving an indelible impression: Hughes manically washing his hands in a public lavatory and then being afraid to open the germ-laden door; Hepburn coming to Hughes in his most reclusive state and compassionately talking to him through the locked door, and many more.

Re-enactments of famous people are always difficult to carry off. Blanchett, though not a dead ringer for Hepburn, captures her voice and mannerisms impressively, and Jude Law's a passable Errol Flynn, though Gwen Stefani and Kate Beckinsale are a far cry from the real Jean Harlow and Gardner. Ace film buff Scorsese should have known better and risen above the sort of inaccurate casting usually found in made-for-TV films. Ian Holm, John C. Reilly, Danny Huston, Adam Scott, Willem Dafoe and Edward Herrmann all shine in supporting roles.

But above all, it is DiCaprio's film. He etches a totally convincing portrait of a great if tortured visionary.

Because of reoccuring profanity and intermittent crude expressions, and an instance of rough language, as well as implied sexual situations and innuendo, a violent plane crash and brief rear nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
